claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game contains undisclosed generative AI assets in its art and writing.

citations.review_text:
Undisclosed AI art usage.
Throws the game's writing and other assets under suspicion, and even if you're pro-AI, people deserve to know honestly if there's AI assets in the game; Steam requires you declare if you used any AI whatsoever.

Biggest thread about it in the steam forums for the game was deleted. Not a good look.

Instead of backing down and claiming it was temporary assets or some such, dev has kept all assets in for months and has even stated his use of it in interviews. He just doesn't want to declare it on the Steam store page for the game, likely because there's a large financial incentive to not declare until players realize they've seen that same AI generated midjourney painting a few times already after it's too late to refund.

Dev quote:
"We are using different technologies, including AI tools, to various degrees – from built-in Photoshop capabilities… Internal Stable Diffusion models, MJ models, pixel correction, scaling solutions and so on… Those are different tools that we use NOT to decrease cost and DEFINITELY NOT to replace artists but to bring better quality to our customers and enhance creativity by allowing faster prototyping and iteration."

So fully capable of admitting it in interviews, still willing to break Steam's terms to falsely advertise their game.

For what it's worth, what I've played mechanically is pretty solid. I think if the dev removed the AI art assets (which shouldn't be an issue -- they have artists on payroll) and came clean about how deeply it's in the game, this game would absolutely be worth your time. In the meantime though, it feels like the deeper into the game I go, the more AI art appears and the stilt-ier the dialogue gets.
There should be a disclosure of Ai usage, by the first cutscene it's obvious Gen Ai was heavily used in every aspect of this game.

I was seriously excited for this game as a big Bethesda game fan throughout the years thinking that a scrolls-like from a studio with fresh ideas might be what it takes to reinvigorate this style of RPG that I love. However, buyer beware, this game is riddled with undisclosed AI. 

Art is very clearly AI, especially with the Sanctuary of Sarras DLC. It became bleedingly obvious to me after starting the game and looking at these wildly different art assets with this very strange stylistic disconnect so I did some digging. Turns out Awaken Realms is a massive supporter of AI in their board game art assets and use it very liberally, something that some folks have found out they are doing with their game development business as well after emailing them about it. 

Now you may have whatever point of view you like about AI in game development, but it is undeniable that they are being disingenuous by not disclosing their usage of it to possible buyers. AI in development pipelines is nothing new, just used to be called machine learning, but AI has no place in the creativity of game development where something so promising like Tainted Grail can be so ironically tainted by it's usage of AI in it's art and writing. 

Me personally, I'm just not interested in AI slop in my RPGs. Buyer beware.

The combat system revolves around blocking and striking. The problem is that the janky a** combat system doesn’t make it clear when you’re supposed to block. “Just before the enemy strikes” is what you’re told but that’s a matter of interpretation rather than something that’s clearly telegraphed. Blocking also has less value when you’re getting mobbed by a group of five or six enemies, which happens with some frequency.

To make matters worse, health potions are hard to come by and the fast travel system is less forgiving than in most games. The result is that the gameplay loop becomes: kill two or three bandits, get severely injured, spend 15 minutes hobbling back to town, spend another 15 minutes getting back to where you were, kill another two or three bandits, and repeat. If that appeals to you, great! But I can’t say it worked for me.

Then you get to the goal where you fight the same human ai but with 2 extra spells and a dash, but the same animations and sometimes the same voicelines! 

In conclusion this game has some pretty cool lore, atmosphere, and dialogue. But the graphics, animations, and AI really pull you out of the immersion.

Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon ended up being one of those games that completely pulled me in, burned me out, and then somehow made me want to come back anyway.

The biggest strength for me was the amount of content. Exploration is constantly rewarded with new quests, strange situations, hidden areas, and side stories, and it has that Skyrim-style feeling where you leave to do one thing and completely forget about it because you found something more interesting along the way.

Combat was fun, although by the end my dash-heavy build made a lot of fights pretty easy. I finished at level 55 on Normal difficulty and definitely felt overpowered during the final stretch.

The game also has some jank, but I never ran into anything game-breaking. After a while, the weird animations and occasional ridiculous enemy deaths just became part of the experience.

My biggest issue was burnout. I tried to do so much that around 60 hours I stopped playing completely. After finishing a couple shorter games, though, I actually wanted to come back. That made me realize I wasn't tired of Tainted Grail itself—I had just tried to take in way too much of it at once.

Unfortunately, the ending was probably the weakest part of my entire 71.8-hour playthrough. The final boss was lackluster, the ending felt rushed, and after spending that much time in the world, my reaction was basically, “That's it?”

Even with that disappointment, I still recommend it. I had way too much fun during the rest of the game for a weak ending to erase the journey.

If you like big open-world RPGs with tons of exploration and side content, Tainted Grail is absolutely worth checking out.

Thumbs Up.

Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon is an amazing open‑world ARPG. Think Skyrim, but smaller in scope, much darker in atmosphere, and with far better combat thanks to its excellent dodge‑based system.

The early game can feel tough, but once you start completing side quests you’ll quickly grow stronger. By the end of the second area you should have solid gear and be able to handle anything the game throws at you. There’s also a NG+ mode that seems to offer fresh challenge—I still need to dive into it.

My only real complaint is that some parts—like the epilogue—could have used more development, but considering the game’s budget, it still delivers a strong experience.

The DLC adds more content and a few interesting characters, but it’s not essential and doesn’t impact the main story. If you do play it, I recommend doing so before finishing Area 2; otherwise it becomes a bit too easy.

Performance-wise, the game runs well and has few bugs. I did have two occasions where I had to use the “unstuck” option because I got caught in the terrain, and I experienced two crashes — both during the DLC. Outside of that, the experience was smooth.

Good game ? Yes. Would I reccommend it ? Yes. But it has it's flaws ? Also yes.

Things why you should play: 
* Very good story, myterious and it's slowly revealing, not cliche.
* There are some good hit mechanics, you feel that you hit enemy and dodging feels fun (at first)
* There is both parry and block mechanic
* There are so many different classes instead of just 3-4 old main rpg classes like mage-warrior-assasin.
* Animations are okay.
* Some of the side quests are really cool, it's not like just go and kill this, they're nice and interesting.

Things which has bothered me (does not have to bother you but probably will):
* Dodging mechanic is a bit broken and op, reducing fights into dodge dodge dodge because why would you try to risk parrying or why would you block when you can easily dodge ?
* You can almost dodge forever, maybe also i played mage, dodge dodge, firebolt, dodge dodge firebolt feels a bit clunky after a while.
* Shield spell is not good enough to make you stop using dodge plus why would you use shield when you can dodge free
* Conjuration is cool at first but later it gets keep conjuring 321312 times to defeat a boss.
* Map is cool but not great. It doesn't have good details, mostly simple.

I love this. The devs have looked at Skyrim and decided 'What if the combat was crunchy and satisfying, the UI was accessible and painless and the world was constantly bizarre and inventive?'. 

The combat is great. Landing a blow feels weighty and meaningful, and physics is turned way up so your defeated foes ragdoll away into beautifully ludicrous shapes. You can block and parry, your enemies have weakspots you can exploit, and you have a lovely whooshy dash for engineering backstabs and getting out of trouble. If magic's your thing, prepare to start slow but balloon into an absolute beast. And stealth archer is a beautiful build. Bows go twang right? Here, bows go twang schoop BANG HISSSSSSSS. 

The world is smaller than Skyrim's, but far more focussed, and less interested in creating a real world setting. If you liked the weirdness of Morrowind, this goes way further.

The QoL additions are lovely - crafting right out of your stash for instance, and having a portable bonfire you can magically charge to send items home, fixing the OCD trudge back to a trader every time you have too many cuirasses in your backpack. Being able to equip sword and shield with a single button press. Being able to take potions to completely rebuild your character from the ground up. citations.review_text:
I have almost 100 hours in Tainted Grail. That probably sounds like a recommendation. It is not.

I tend to finish what I start, even when it turns into "grit your teeth and get it over with" instead of fun.

With Tainted Grail, the fun mostly wore off after maybe 10-20 hours. After that, the game survived on one thought: "There has to be more to this."

There is not.

And that is my biggest problem with the game: [b]Tainted Grail is a facade.[/b]

The first few hours work surprisingly well. Everywhere you look are systems that seem full of potential: a huge skill tree, cooking, fishing, alchemy, crafting, tons of items and ingredients, armor weight, status effects, factions, choices, exploration and loot.

At first it looks like a huge RPG full of possibilities. Eventually you realize that this is basically it.

Almost every system has a foundation, but very few are properly developed or meaningfully connected. The developers simply bit off more than they could chew. Five well-designed systems that interact and develop throughout the game would have been much better than ten half-baked ones.

A lot of it feels like ready-made building blocks and assets made to work technically, without enough thought about what to do with them afterwards. I do not know what was bought or made in-house; I am describing how it feels to play.

Very often the game seems to say: "Look, we have this too!"

Okay. Now what?

[b]Cooking and fishing[/b]

There are tons of ingredients and dozens of recipes, yet very early in Act 1 I already had a simple three-fish recipe restoring 120 HP at base quality. Many hours and exotic ingredients later, much more elaborate dishes are barely better. I ate that beginner dish for practically the entire game.

It even scales with cooking quality: the same dirt-cheap recipe went from 120 HP at base quality to 125 HP at +1 and 138 HP at +3. Instead of later recipes replacing it through meaningful progression, the early recipe simpl…

A proof that small teams can make games akin to Elder Scrolls series. Interesting setting, quality art and ok writing. 

Biggest downsides are that the gameplay itself after few hours becomes an afterthought since its extremely easy to become overpowered and the game morphs into walking sim even on the highest difficulty level. Many of the gameplay systems are there mostly to check checkboxes and with surface level depth. This includes, cooking, alchemy, smithing, etc. The “level-as-you-use” skills can be safely ignored since the bonuses they provided are so minuscule you will never notice them. 

Regarding the game itself, it consists of 3 acts where each act is different open world map containing dungeons, towns and camps. From those, act 1 is inconsistent tone wise, act 2 is the strongest and the act 3 feels heavily padded. 

I feel if the game had better focus and was a tad bit shorter, it would go from good to great.

citations.review_text: Good game with great story and roleplaying. From a technical standpoint it's just ok. Expect bugs and save often. For quality of life improvements like a minimap, inventory sorting and categories, loot filtering and summon behaviour switching to the Mono version and using mods is recommended. Balancing is still off even after the introduction of diminishing returns on the effects of attribute points: once my summoner build came to life it was a walk in the park on Veteran difficulty and it only got easier after that. Because of bugs I also cannot recommend Survival Mode: it restricts saving to rests at beds and fireplaces which is infuriating when you encounter quest progression bugs or simply fall through the map. Nevertheless, I had many hours of fun in the game so it's a clean recommendation.

Ups: It's the Rare game that seems to get Lovecraftian story telling while being very open and fun to play.

Downs: The actual script is pretty weak, the graphics lean on dull, washed out colors and it is glitchy, even the ending broke cut scenes broke.

On the whole, it's an easy recommend, especially with Mods. Just save frequently and keep multiple files.
